title: The Place He Will Choose
sum: The law code begins. Moses tells Israel to destroy every Canaanite shrine "on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every leafy tree" (12:2), and not to worship the LORD in the same way. Instead they must bring their offerings, tithes and vows to "the place the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there" (12:5), and eat there with joy, sharing with their slaves and the Levite. Because sacrifice is now limited to one place, ordinary meat may be slaughtered and eaten in any town, as long as the blood is poured out (12:15–25). The chapter ends with a warning not to copy the nations, who "even burn their sons and their daughters" for their gods (12:31), and not to add to the commands or take away from them (12:32).
Almost everything in chapters 12–26 depends on this chapter. Tithes, firstborn animals, feasts and high courts all point back to "the place."
readings: Read as a reform

The chapter reads like a program of change. "Do not do all that we are doing here today, each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (12:8) admits that worship has been local and varied. The law closes the many altars and opens the towns to everyday butchering. Joy is commanded, and the circle of joy includes slaves and Levites.
Read as theology

Behind the rule lies a claim about God. The nations worship many gods in many places; Israel worships one God in the place he chooses. God does not live there in a simple way: he puts his "name" there. The God who is one must be worshiped as one, and on his terms, not on borrowed ones (12:30–31).

views.H: Moses, on the plains of Moab, looks ahead to settled life in the land. He leaves the place unnamed because it is not yet chosen. Traditional readers see the tabernacle at Shiloh and then the temple at Jerusalem as the fulfillment (Jeremiah 7:12; 1 Kings 8:29).
views.C: Most scholars see this chapter as the heart of Josiah's reform in 622 BC, when local shrines were closed and worship moved to Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:8–9). The chapter has several overlapping versions of the same command (12:2–7, 8–12, 13–19, 20–28), which many read as layers added over time.
views.T: Assyrian loyalty oaths demanded exclusive loyalty to one king and his chosen heir. Deuteronomy applies the same demand to worship: one LORD, one place, no rival practice. Weinfeld noted that the ban on adding to the commands or taking away from them (12:32) is treaty language.
views.J: The rabbis drew from this chapter the rule that sacrifices could be offered only at the temple once it was built (Mishnah Zevachim 14:4–8). From 12:21, "as I have commanded you," the Talmud derived the laws of ritual slaughter, which Moses must have taught orally (Chullin 28a). Since the temple fell, no sacrifices are offered at all.
views.X: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that "neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem" will the Father be worshiped, but "in spirit and truth" (John 4:21–24). Christians read the chosen place as fulfilled in Christ himself, the true temple (John 2:19–21).

deep.b: Before this law, killing an animal for food may have been treated as a sacrifice (Leviticus 17:3–7 requires every slaughtered ox or sheep to be brought to the tent). Once worship moves to one distant place, that rule cannot work. Deuteronomy allows "profane slaughter": meat may be eaten in any town, by clean and unclean alike, "as they would a gazelle or a deer," wild game that was never sacrificed. The one rule that stays is the blood, which belongs to God because "the blood is the life" (12:23).

Many readers notice that 12:8 speaks of "all that we are doing here today." If this is Moses in the wilderness, it means that Israel's worship was already varied in his time. If it is a later voice, it admits that the old ways of worship in Israel had been plural. Either way, the law presents itself as a change, not as the way things always were.

echoes: Exodus 20:24; Leviticus 17:1–9; Joshua 18:1; Judges 17:6; 1 Kings 8:29; 2 Kings 23:1–25; Jeremiah 7:12; John 4:20–24; Revelation 22:18–19

settings.what: The law code: rules for life in the land
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, for life in the land: every household, the town elders and judges, the priests and Levites, the prophets and the king
settings.when: given before the crossing, to take effect "in the land" for as long as Israel lives on its soil (12:1)
settings.why: The laws are not for the wilderness camp but for settled life in the land. Many scholars, following Kaufman, think they follow roughly the order of the Ten Words; others see other plans, such as the move to one place of worship. Worship comes first: one place, one God, holy food and tithes, release of debts and the feasts (12:1–16:17). Then the offices: judges, the king, priests and Levites, and prophets (16:18–18:22). Then laws on life and death, war, family, neighbors, the poor and the weak (19–25), and last the first fruits (26). Again and again the reason given is memory: "Remember that you were a slave in Egypt" (16:12).
views: Traditional readers take the code as Moses' explanation of the Sinai law, adapted for life in the land.

Many critical scholars, especially Levinson, see the code as a deliberate rewriting of the older laws of Exodus 21–23. It was made for Judah in the 7th century BC, to serve Josiah's reform of worship around Jerusalem.
Others trace the core of the code to northern Israel before 722 BC, brought south by Levites or prophets.

settings.what: Worship at the one place the LORD will choose
settings.to: Every Israelite household, once Israel is settled in the land and has rest from its enemies (12:10)
settings.why: Israel must tear down every Canaanite shrine. It must bring all sacrifices, tithes and vows to "the place the LORD your God will choose" (12:5). There households rejoice with their slaves and the Levite. Sacrifice is now limited to one place. So ordinary meat may be killed and eaten in any town, if the blood is poured out. The problem the law answers is worship mixed with the gods of the land. The place is not named. Later Israel saw it as Shiloh first, then Jerusalem.
views: Most critical scholars connect this law with Hezekiah's and Josiah's efforts to close the shrines outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 23:8–9).
Any place God chooses in turn
Some read "the place" as whatever sanctuary God chose in each period, such as Shiloh and later Jerusalem. Schenker notes that some old witnesses read "has chosen."

title: When the Sign Comes True
sum: Chapter 13 takes on three threats to loyalty. First, a prophet or dreamer gives a sign that comes true, then says, "Let us follow other gods." Israel must not listen, "for the LORD your God is testing you" (13:3), and the prophet must die. Second, a close family member or friend "may try to lure you in secret" (13:6). No pity, no cover: "your hand is to be the first against him" (13:9). Third, a whole town is led astray by "worthless men" (13:13). After careful inquiry, the town is put under the ban and burned as "a ruin-mound for all time" (13:16).
The chapter is among the harshest in the Bible. It shows how seriously Deuteronomy treats exclusive loyalty to the LORD, and it raised hard questions for later Jewish and Christian readers.
readings: Read as a loyalty oath

The structure follows ancient treaty clauses about rebellion: if you hear treason from a prophet, a relative or a town, you must report or punish it. The covenant is treated like a political allegiance, and turning to other gods is treason.
Read as a test of truth

The first case makes a lasting point: a true prediction does not prove a true prophet. What a prophet teaches about God matters more than what he can do. Later Jewish and Christian tradition used this test against wonder-workers who led people away.

views.H: Moses speaks of dangers the people will face in the land. The harsh penalties guard the life of a nation newly bound to God. Traditional interpreters, following the rabbis, read the chapter as requiring a court and witnesses (13:14; 17:6), though the Hebrew of 13:9 can be read as allowing immediate killing (see the variant).
views.C: The chapter is one of the clearest borrowings from Assyrian loyalty oaths, especially Esarhaddon's succession treaty of 672 BC, which requires vassals to report anyone, even a brother or prophet, who speaks against the crown prince. Levinson and others see Deuteronomy turning that oath toward the LORD.
views.T: The parallels with Esarhaddon's treaty are close in order and wording: prophet, ecstatic or dream-reader; brother, son or daughter; the duty to seize and kill. Here the LORD takes the place of the Assyrian king.
views.J: The rabbis said the town of 13:12–18 "never was and never will be," and that it was written so that one might study it and receive reward (Sanhedrin 71a). They required that most of the town have worshiped idols and that the town not be a border town (Sanhedrin 16b), Jerusalem (Bava Kamma 82b) or a city of refuge.
views.X: Jesus warns that false prophets will "give great signs and wonders" (Matthew 24:24), and Paul writes that even an angel preaching another gospel is to be cursed (Galatians 1:8). Most Christians today do not apply the penalties of this chapter, reading them as belonging to Israel's covenant state. But for centuries the chapter was used to justify executing heretics: Augustine cited Old Testament penalties against the Donatists, Calvin argued from it after the burning of Servetus (1553–54), and Puritan law codes such as the Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) cited it for idolatry. Roger Williams (The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution, 1644) and the Anabaptists answered that the church's only sword is the word. See the note on 13:10.

deep.b: The Hebrew of 13:9 says "you must kill him"; the Greek translation says "you must report him." The difference matters. The Greek fits a trial before witnesses (17:6); the Hebrew sounds like instant justice. Bernard Levinson argued that the Hebrew is original because Esarhaddon's oath also required vassals to seize and kill traitors. See the variant on this verse.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:2–7; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Joshua 7; Judges 20; 1 Kings 18:40; Matthew 24:24; Galatians 1:8–9; 2 Thessalonians 2:9–12; 1 John 4:1

settings.what: Three tempters to other gods
settings.to: Every Israelite, and the town elders and the whole community as judges, in the land
settings.why: The law deals with three threats to loyalty. One is a prophet whose sign comes true. One is a close family member who tempts in secret. One is a whole town led astray. The test of a prophet is not whether his sign works but whether he leads to the LORD. These laws bind even the family. The chapter is among the harshest in the Bible. Later Jews and Christians argued about how, and whether, to apply it.
views: Weinfeld and Levinson note that the vassal oaths of Esarhaddon (672 BC) also require reporting even a brother or a son who plots against the king. Deuteronomy turns that loyalty to the LORD.

title: A People Holy to the LORD
sum: "You are children of the LORD your God" (14:1). Because Israel is "a people holy to the LORD" and his "own private treasure" (14:2), it must not cut itself or shave its head for the dead, and must not eat what is "abhorrent." The chapter lists clean animals, including wild game, gives the signs of clean land animals, fish and birds, and forbids eating an animal that has died on its own. It repeats the old command, "Do not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother" (14:21).

The second half turns to the tithe. A tenth of the crops is eaten by the household at the chosen place, or turned into silver and spent there on "cattle, sheep, wine, beer, or anything else you would like" (14:26). Every third year it is stored in the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.
readings: Read as identity

Food marks a people. Twice the chapter names Israel "holy to the LORD," at its start and at the end of the food list (14:2, 21). What Israel does not eat sets it apart from the nations, just as its refusal to mourn like them does.
Read as celebration

The tithe here is a feast, not a tax. A farmer takes his household to the chosen place and eats and drinks "before the LORD" with joy, so that "you will learn to fear the LORD your God always" (14:23). Even the poor and the Levite are given their share every third year.

views.H: Moses repeats the food laws given at Sinai (Leviticus 11) in shorter form for the whole people about to enter the land, adding the wild game they will hunt there.
views.C: Many scholars think Deuteronomy 14 and Leviticus 11 both draw on an older list. Deuteronomy's tithe, eaten by the farmer, differs from the Levites' tithe in Numbers 18, which suggests different periods or circles of writers.
views.T: Treaty vassals were often called the great king's "servants" or "sons." "Children of the LORD" and "own private treasure" (a term used of a king's personal property in Ugaritic texts) express a special status within the covenant.
views.J: The rabbis read "do not boil a young goat" three times in the Torah (Exodus 23:19; 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21) as forbidding cooking, eating and benefiting from meat with milk (Chullin 115b). Kosher kitchens still separate meat and dairy. The tithe laws became the "second tithe" and the "tithe for the poor."
views.X: Peter's vision of clean and unclean animals (Acts 10:9–16) and Mark's comment that Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19) led most Christians to set aside the food laws, while keeping their call to be a holy people (1 Peter 1:15–16).

deep.b: Readers have offered many explanations. Some, like Maimonides, pointed to health. Philo and the Letter of Aristeas read the animals as moral symbols: chewing the cud is like reflecting on wisdom. Mary Douglas argued that clean animals are those that fit their category of creation, while animals that cross categories are unclean. Others see a rejection of animals linked with foreign worship, such as the pig. Deuteronomy itself gives one reason: "you are a people holy to the LORD."

echoes: Leviticus 11; Leviticus 19:27–28; Leviticus 27:30–33; Numbers 18:21–32; Exodus 19:5–6; Exodus 23:19; Acts 10:9–16; Mark 7:19; 1 Peter 1:15–16; 1 Peter 2:9

settings.what: A holy people at the table and in mourning
settings.to: Every Israelite household, in daily life in the land
settings.why: Israel is "a people holy to the LORD" (14:2). So it must not cut itself or shave its head for the dead, and it must eat only clean animals. The list follows Leviticus 11 closely but adds wild game, which fits life in the land. An animal that died on its own may be given to the foreigner who lives in Israel, or sold to an outsider. The food laws bind Israel, not them.

settings.what: Tithes: eaten with joy, shared with the poor
settings.to: Israelite farmers and households in the land
settings.when: every year, and every third year
settings.why: Each year the household eats a tenth of its crops at the chosen place. Or it turns the tenth into silver and spends it there on a feast. Every third year the tithe is stored in the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. The problem it answers is who will feed those with no land. Worship and care for the poor are one law.

traditions.q: Moses lets the family buy wine and beer for the feast (14:26). May Christians drink alcohol?
views: Yes, in moderation. Wine is a good gift of God and is required for the Eucharist, while drunkenness is a sin (Catechism 2290).
Yes. Wine is used in the Eucharist and at feasts, and the Orthodox give it up on many fast days as a discipline.

Wesley's General Rules (1743) forbade drunkenness and the buying, selling or drinking of spirits except in real need. American Methodists led the temperance movement and began using grape juice for communion in the 1800s, and many Methodists still urge abstinence.

Baptists are divided. The Southern Baptist Convention has passed resolutions urging total abstinence and uses grape juice at the Lord's Supper; many other Baptists drink in moderation and point to verses like this one and Jesus' wine at Cana (John 2:1–11).
Adventists abstain completely from alcohol, as well as tobacco, to keep the body a temple of the Holy Spirit (Fundamental Beliefs 22).
Latter-day Saints do not drink alcohol, following the Word of Wisdom revealed in 1833 (Doctrine and Covenants 89).

title: Open Your Hand
sum: Every seventh year is a "release" (15:1). Lenders must cancel loans to fellow Israelites. "There will be no one in need among you" if Israel obeys (15:4), but since need will never disappear, Israel must not "harden your heart or close your hand" (15:7), nor refuse a loan because the release year is near. "Open your hand wide to your brother" (15:11).

A Hebrew slave, man or woman, goes free after six years and must not leave "with empty hands" (15:13). A slave who wants to stay has his ear pierced at the door. Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD and are eaten at the chosen place, unless they have a defect.
readings: Read as economics

The chapter is a social safety net. Debt slavery and endless debt were common in the ancient world. The release year cancels debts, the seventh year frees slaves, and the gifts at release give a fresh start. Its success depends on lenders' willingness to keep lending.
Read as spirituality

The law speaks to the heart: no "worthless thought," no resentment, a hand that opens. Generosity is not only a duty but a response to grace: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God ransomed you" (15:15).

views.H: Moses expands the seventh-year laws given at Sinai (Exodus 21:2–11; Exodus 23:10–11) for settled life in a land of farms and loans.
views.C: The chapter revises Exodus 21. It adds women to the release, removes Exodus's rule that a slave's wife given by the master stays behind, and drops Exodus's "bring him to God" (Exodus 21:6), so the ear-piercing becomes a household act at the door. Scholars see a reform that makes the law more humane and less tied to the sanctuary.
views.T: Babylonian kings sometimes proclaimed a "release" (misharum) of debts at their accession. Deuteronomy makes such a release regular and makes it the LORD's decree, not a king's favor.
views.J: When the release year made lenders stop lending, Hillel created the prozbul, a document assigning loans to the court so that they survived the release (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3–4). The law of release is still kept in a limited form in Israel, mainly for farmland.
views.X: Jesus quotes 15:11 when Mary anoints him: "you have the poor among you at all times" (Mark 14:7). The early church's sharing, so that "nobody among them was in need" (Acts 4:34), echoes 15:4.

deep.h: No one in need, or always people in need?
deep.b: Verse 4 promises that there will be no poor; verse 11 says the poor will never cease. The two belong together. Verse 4 describes what the land would be if Israel fully obeyed; verse 11 admits that it will not. The command that follows each is the same: lend, give, open your hand. The law refuses both easy hope and easy despair.

echoes: Exodus 21:2–11; Exodus 23:10–11; Leviticus 25; Nehemiah 10:31; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Mark 14:7; Acts 4:34; 2 Corinthians 9:7

settings.what: The year of release: cancel the debts
settings.to: Israelite lenders, every seventh year, in the land
settings.why: At the end of every seven years, loans to fellow Israelites must be canceled; a foreigner's debt may still be collected. The goal is that there be no one in need among you (15:4). Yet Moses knows need will not disappear. So he warns against refusing loans as the year draws near. "Open your hand wide to your brother" (15:11). The law answers the debt that pushed poor farmers into slavery.
views: The rabbis took the release as a full cancellation. Later they allowed Hillel's prosbul to keep credit flowing. Some modern scholars think it only paused repayment for a year.

settings.what: Freeing Hebrew slaves
settings.to: Israelite masters, men and women, in the land
settings.when: in the seventh year of a slave's service
settings.why: A Hebrew slave, man or woman, goes free after six years and must not leave with empty hands. The master must give from flock, grain floor and wine press. A slave who wants to stay has his ear pierced at the door. The reason: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (15:15). Many scholars think the law revises Exodus 21:2–11 to treat the woman slave as the man. Others think Exodus 21:7–11, on a daughter sold as a wife, deals with a different case.

settings.what: Firstborn animals
settings.to: Israelite herders and households in the land
settings.why: Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD and are eaten each year at the chosen place. A firstborn with a defect may be eaten at home like ordinary meat. The law fits the old rule of the firstborn to the new rule of one place of worship.

title: Three Times a Year
sum: Israel's three pilgrim feasts are kept at the chosen place. Passover is held in the month of Abib, with unleavened bread, "the bread of hardship," for seven days (16:3). Seven weeks later comes the Feast of Weeks, with a freewill offering. In the autumn comes the Feast of Booths, seven days of joy. "No one is to appear before the LORD with empty hands" (16:16).

The chapter then turns to justice. Judges are to be appointed in every town, take no bribes, and "Justice, justice is what you must pursue" (16:20). It ends by forbidding Asherah poles and standing stones beside the LORD's altar.
readings: Read as a calendar

The feasts follow the farming year: barley at Passover, wheat at Weeks, fruit and grapes at Booths. Each is joined to memory, especially of Egypt, and each is shared with servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows.
Read as a constitution
Verses 16:18–18:22 set out the offices of Israel: judges, high court, king, priests and prophets. This section begins with the judges because justice is the first duty of any society.

views.H: Moses gives the feasts in a form suited to life in the land. Passover, first kept in homes in Egypt, now becomes a national feast at the sanctuary.
views.C: Deuteronomy moves Passover from the home (Exodus 12) to the central sanctuary. 2 Kings 23:22 says no Passover like Josiah's had been held since the judges, which many read as the first Passover kept by this law.
views.T: Vassals were required to appear before the great king with tribute at set times. Israel's three pilgrimages with gifts in hand resemble those visits, but the tone is joy rather than duty.
views.J: The doubled "justice, justice" was read as a call to pursue justice by just means (Rabbi Simcha Bunim) and to seek a good court (Sanhedrin 32b). The feasts remain the three pilgrimage festivals: Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot.
views.X: Jesus went to Jerusalem for Passover and Booths (Luke 2:41; John 7:2–10). The Spirit came on the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost (Acts 2:1), and Christians link Jesus' death to Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

deep.b: Exodus says a bribe "blinds those who see clearly" (Exodus 23:8). Deuteronomy says it "blinds the eyes of the wise and turns the words of the righteous upside down" (16:19). Not even the best judges are immune. Rabbinic law forbade a judge to accept even a small kindness from a party in a case (Ketubot 105b).

echoes: Exodus 12; Exodus 23:6–8, 14–17; Exodus 34:18–24; Leviticus 23; Numbers 28–29; 2 Kings 23:21–23; Luke 2:41; John 7:2; Acts 2:1

settings.what: Three pilgrim feasts
settings.to: Every Israelite man three times a year, with his household, the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, at the chosen place
settings.when: Passover in the month of Abib, Weeks seven weeks later, Booths in the autumn
settings.why: Passover, Weeks and Booths are kept at the one place, not at home. Passover becomes a pilgrim feast. Weeks and Booths are times of joy. They are shared with slaves, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows (16:11, 14). No one may come with empty hands. The law turns the farmer's year into a memory of Egypt and a meal with the poor.
views: Josiah ordered the people to hold a Passover "by what is written in this covenant scroll" (2 Kings 23:21). It was the first like it since the judges (2 Kings 23:22). Many critical scholars see this law behind that national Passover in Jerusalem.

settings.what: The offices: judges, king, priests and prophets
settings.to: The whole people, who appoint judges and may set a king over themselves, and the officials who hold these offices in the land
settings.why: This section shares power among four offices. Judges serve in every town and at the central court. The king is chosen by God and bound by the written law. The Levite priests serve at the altar and teach. Prophets speak the LORD's word. No office stands above the law. Scholars have called it the first constitution, because the law limits even the king. It answers the question of who will lead Israel when Moses is gone.

settings.what: Judges in every town
settings.to: The people of each town, who appoint judges and officials, and the judges themselves
settings.when: once Israel is living in its towns in the land
settings.why: Judges must judge fairly, show no favoritism and take no bribe. "Justice, justice is what you must pursue" (16:20). Life in the land depends on it. The law moves justice from the elders of the clan toward appointed judges in each town.

settings.what: Pure worship, and trials for worshiping other gods
settings.to: Israelite worshipers, and the town and its judges who must try the case
settings.why: No Asherah pole or standing stone may stand by the LORD's altar, and no blemished animal may be offered. Anyone who worships other gods, or the sun, moon and stars, must be tried with care. The charge must be investigated, and no one may die on the word of one witness. The law protects worship and the accused at once.

title: A King Under the Law
sum: After a ban on blemished sacrifices, the chapter sets out how to judge anyone who worships other gods, "the sun or the moon or any of the army of the heavens" (17:3). The charge must be investigated, and no one may die "on the word of one witness" (17:6). Cases too hard for local courts go to the Levite priests and the judge at the chosen place, whose ruling must be followed.

Then comes the only law of kingship in the Torah. Israel may set a king over itself, but he must be chosen by God and be an Israelite. He must not multiply horses, wives or silver and gold. He must write a copy of "this law" and read it "all the days of his life" (17:19), so that his heart "will not be lifted up above his brothers" (17:20).
readings: Read as politics

The king's law is a bold limit on power in a world of god-kings. Israel's king has no special role in war, courts or worship here. He is one of the brothers, bound by the same written law as everyone else.
Read as a portrait of Solomon

Each limit matches a fault of Solomon: horses from Egypt, seven hundred wives who turned his heart, and gold so plentiful that silver was counted as nothing (1 Kings 10:21–11:4). The law reads like a judgment on the most glorious king.

views.H: Moses foresees that Israel will one day ask for a king and gives rules in advance. When Israel does ask, "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5), Samuel's warning echoes this law.
views.C: Many scholars date the law of the king to the late monarchy or the exile, written with the failures of the kings in view, especially Solomon. Its view that the king's only duty is to study the law looks like a later ideal.
views.T: Treaties bound vassal kings to their overlords. In Deuteronomy the human king is himself a vassal of the LORD, required to keep a copy of the covenant document, as vassals kept copies of their treaties.
views.J: The rabbis debated whether appointing a king was a command or a concession (Sanhedrin 20b). The Mishnah says the king writes his own scroll and carries it with him (Mishnah Sanhedrin 2:4); the Talmud adds a second kept in his treasury (Sanhedrin 21b). The Greek translation's name for this book, Deuteronomium, "second law," comes from its rendering of 17:18, "a copy of this law."
views.X: Christians see Jesus as the true king who did not multiply wealth or power, but "humbled himself" (Philippians 2:8). Jesus' answer that his kingdom is "not of this world" (John 18:36) stands in the same tradition of limited earthly power.

deep.b: In 17:18 the Hebrew mishneh hattorah hazzot means "a copy of this law." The Greek translators wrote to deuteronomion touto, "this second law," and the name stuck to the whole book. The rabbis also called it Mishneh Torah, "the repetition of the law."

echoes: 1 Samuel 8; 1 Samuel 10:25; 1 Kings 10:14–11:8; 2 Kings 22:8–13; Psalm 72; Isaiah 11:1–5; Matthew 18:16; John 18:36

settings.what: The high court at the chosen place
settings.to: Local judges with cases too hard for them, and the Levite priests and the judge at the central sanctuary
settings.why: Hard cases of bloodshed, rights and injury go up to the chosen place. There the Levite priests and the judge in office give a ruling that must be followed. The law answers the problem of cases that a town court cannot settle. Under the critical view, it fits a time when local shrines were closed and justice was centered in Jerusalem.

settings.what: The law of the king
settings.to: The people, who may set a king over themselves, and every future king of Israel
settings.when: looking ahead to when Israel says, "I will set a king over me"
settings.why: This is the only law of kingship in the Torah. The king must be chosen by God and be an Israelite. He must not gather many horses, wives, or silver and gold, and he must not send the people back to Egypt. He must write a copy of this law and read it all the days of his life. Then his heart will not be lifted up above his brothers (17:18–20). The law answers the danger of a king like the kings of the nations, or like Solomon (1 Kings 10:26–11:4).
views: Traditional readers see Moses foreseeing the request of 1 Samuel 8 and setting limits in advance.

Many critical scholars read the law against Solomon's excess and the kings of Judah. Josiah heard the scroll read and obeyed it, so he fits the model king (2 Kings 23:25). Pakkala and others think the law, which gives the king almost nothing to do, fits a time after the kings were gone.

title: A Prophet Like Me
sum: The Levite priests have no land; "The LORD is their inheritance" (18:2). They receive parts of the sacrifices and the first of the harvest and wool, and any Levite who comes to the chosen place may serve there with his fellow Levites.

Moses then forbids the practices of the nations: child sacrifice, divination, omens, sorcery, spells and consulting the dead. In their place, "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me" (18:15), as Israel asked at Horeb when it feared to hear God's voice. A prophet who speaks a word God did not command must die, and a prediction that fails shows a false prophet.
readings: Read as the gift of prophecy
The chapter answers a basic human desire to know what is coming. The nations seek it through magic and the dead. Israel receives it through a person God sends, who speaks God's words.
Read as messianic promise
Read alongside 34:10, which says no prophet like Moses ever arose again in Israel, the promise points forward. Samaritans, the Qumran community and early Christians all looked for one coming Prophet.

views.H: Moses promises the line of prophets that will follow him, beginning with Joshua and continuing through Samuel, Elijah and the rest. Traditional Christians add that the promise reaches its fullness in Jesus.
views.C: Scholars see here a theory of prophecy from the circles that produced Deuteronomy, who saw Moses as the first and greatest prophet. The test of failed predictions (18:22) became important after the exile, when people asked which prophets had been right.
views.T: Assyrian kings consulted diviners about every decision, and their treaties demanded that vassals report any word of a prophet against the king. Deuteronomy replaces divination with prophecy that comes from the covenant Lord himself.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the promise as fulfilled in each true prophet. Maimonides lists belief that Moses' prophecy was greater than all others among his thirteen principles. The Levites' portions (18:3) became the priestly gifts still discussed in Jewish law (Chullin 130a).
views.X: Peter quotes 18:15 and 18:19 in the temple to say that Jesus is the promised prophet (Acts 3:22–23), and Stephen does the same (Acts 7:37). At the transfiguration the voice says, "listen to him" (Mark 9:7), echoing "You must listen to him."

deep.b: The terms in 18:10–11 are hard to translate exactly. The ov may have been a pit or spirit of the dead; the yidde'oni a "knowing one" who speaks for them. Saul asked the woman of Endor to call up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7–19). Isaiah mocks those who "go to the dead about the living" (Isaiah 8:19). Archaeologists have found offerings to the dead at family tombs in Judah, which shows why the law was needed.

echoes: Numbers 18; Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6, 27; 1 Samuel 28; 2 Kings 21:6; Jeremiah 28:9; Mark 9:7; John 1:21; John 6:14; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37

settings.what: The Levite priests and their share
settings.to: The Levite priests and the whole tribe of Levi, and the Israelites who owe them their dues
settings.why: Levi gets no land: "The LORD is their inheritance" (18:2). The people give the priests parts of the sacrifices and the first of grain, wine, oil and wool. Any Levite from the towns may come to the chosen place and serve there with an equal share. The law answers how a tribe without land will live. It also answers how country Levites will fare when worship moves to one place.
views: 2 Kings 23:9 says the priests of the high places did not come up to the altar in Jerusalem. Many scholars see a tension between this law and what happened in Josiah's reform.

settings.what: No diviners: a prophet like Moses
settings.to: Every Israelite in the land, and those who claim to speak for God
settings.why: Israel must not copy the nations' child sacrifice, divination, sorcery or consulting the dead. Instead, "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me" (18:15). A prophet who speaks in God's name a word that does not come true has not been sent. The law answers how Israel will hear God after Moses dies. Jews have read it of the line of true prophets. Christians also read it of Jesus (Acts 3:22–23).
views: Many Jewish and modern readers take "a prophet" as each true prophet in turn.
Others, in the late Second Temple period and in the New Testament, read it as one prophet like Moses, still to come (34:10; John 1:21).

traditions.q: Is asking the saints to pray for us the same as consulting the dead (18:10–11)?
views: No. The saints are not dead but alive in Christ, since God is the God of the living (Mark 12:27), and asking them to pray is like asking a friend on earth (Catechism 956, 2683). The Church itself forbids calling up the dead and every kind of spiritism (Catechism 2116–2117).

No. The church in heaven and the church on earth are one family in Christ, so Orthodox Christians ask the Mother of God and the saints for their prayers in every service. Necromancy seeks hidden knowledge or power from spirits; prayer to the saints seeks only their prayers.
The saints should be remembered and their faith imitated, but Scripture does not teach calling on them, since Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; Augsburg Confession, article 21).

Prayer is part of worship and is given to God alone, not to angels, saints or any creature (Westminster Confession 21.2). Many Reformed writers see praying to the saints as close to what this passage forbids.

Article 22 calls the invocation of saints a foolish invention with no warrant in Scripture. Anglicans are divided today: evangelicals follow the Article, while many Anglo-Catholics ask for the saints' prayers.

title: Refuge and Witness
sum: Three cities of refuge must be set apart in the land, with roads prepared, so that someone who killed by accident can run there and live. The chapter gives a clear example: an axe head "flies off the handle" and kills a fellow woodcutter (19:5). A murderer who flees to a refuge city must be taken out and handed to the avenger of blood.

Short laws follow: do not move a neighbor's boundary marker; no one may be convicted on the word of one witness; and a false witness receives the punishment he plotted for his victim, "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (19:21).
readings: Read as limits on revenge
In a world where families avenged their dead, the cities of refuge kept an accident from becoming a feud. The law separates intent from outcome and protects the one who did not mean to kill.
Read as protection for the truth

Two witnesses, a careful inquiry, and a heavy penalty for perjury together make courts trustworthy. "Eye for eye" here is applied to the false witness, who is punished by the standard he hoped to use on another.

views.H: Moses has already named three cities east of the Jordan (4:41–43). Here he commands three more for the land west of the Jordan, which Joshua later sets apart (Joshua 20).
views.C: The law adapts the older altar asylum of Exodus 21:13–14 to a time when local altars were closed. Unlike Numbers 35, it does not link the refugee's release to the high priest's death, which suggests a separate tradition.
views.T: Ancient laws often punished false accusers with the penalty of the charge they brought (Hammurabi, Laws 1–4). Deuteronomy shares the principle but rests it on God's presence: the parties stand "before the LORD" (19:17).
views.J: The rabbis required road signs reading "Refuge, refuge" at crossroads (Makkot 10b). They limited the false-witness penalty to cases where the witnesses were proven to have been elsewhere, and only if the accused had not yet been executed (Mishnah Makkot 1:6).
views.X: Jesus requires two or three witnesses in church disputes (Matthew 18:16), and Paul applies the rule to accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus sets "eye for eye" against the call not to resist an evildoer (Matthew 5:38–39).

deep.b: Boundary stones marked family land handed down from the first settlers. Moving one stole from a family for all generations. Proverbs repeats the law (Proverbs 22:28; 23:10), and the curses of 27:17 include it. Babylonian boundary stones, called kudurru, carried curses on anyone who moved them.

echoes: Exodus 21:12–14, 23–25; Leviticus 24:19–20; Numbers 35:9–34; Joshua 20; Proverbs 22:28; Matthew 5:38–39; Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19

settings.what: Towns of refuge for the one who kills by accident
settings.to: The people and town elders in the land, the avenger of blood, and anyone who kills another
settings.when: once the land west of the Jordan is taken
settings.why: Three towns must be set apart west of the Jordan, with roads kept clear. Then someone who kills by accident can flee and live. The example is a woodcutter whose axe head flies off. A murderer who flees there must be handed over by his own town's elders. The law answers blood feud: it keeps innocent blood from being shed in the land.

settings.what: Boundary markers and honest witnesses
settings.to: Every landholder, every witness, and the judges and priests who hear cases in the land
settings.why: No one may move a neighbor's boundary marker, which was set by earlier generations. No one may be convicted on the word of one witness. A false witness gets the punishment he planned for his victim, "life for life, eye for eye" (19:21). The text gives its own reason: "The rest will hear and be afraid" (19:20), and the judges must show no pity. Many readers think the rule of like-for-like also set a limit on punishment.

title: Rules for War
sum: When Israel faces a larger army, it must not fear, for "the LORD your God, who brought you up from the land of Egypt, is with you" (20:1). A priest speaks to the troops, and officials send home anyone who has a new house, an unharvested vineyard or a fiancée, and anyone afraid. Distant cities are first offered peace; those that refuse are besieged, their men killed and the rest taken as spoil.

But in the cities of the land itself, "do not let anything that breathes stay alive" (20:16), so that the nations will not teach Israel their worship. Even in a siege, fruit trees must be spared: "Is the tree of the field a human being, to come under siege from you?" (20:19).
readings: Read as restraint

Compared with Assyrian practice, which boasted of cutting down orchards and flaying captives, these rules limit war: exemptions for soldiers, an offer of peace, protection for trees. Many readers see the beginnings of a law of war.
Read as a moral problem

The command to destroy all who breathe in the cities of Canaan is one of the hardest texts in Scripture. Readers ask how it fits a God of justice and mercy, and whether it describes literal events, rhetoric, or a stage in moral understanding.

views.H: Moses gives Israel rules for the conquest and for later wars. The ban on the Canaanites is God's judgment on their sins (9:4–5; Genesis 15:16) and a protection against idolatry, limited to that time and place.
views.C: Most scholars think the war laws were written centuries after any conquest and that the ban language is an ideal rather than a record. Archaeology does not support a sudden destruction of Canaan's cities, and Judges shows Canaanites living on in the land (Judges 1).
views.T: The Moabite king Mesha's stone inscription (about 840 BC) boasts that he put a whole Israelite town under the ban for his god Kemosh. Israel's ban belongs to a shared ancient practice, now commanded by the LORD.
views.J: The rabbis taught that peace must be offered even to the seven nations, and that a siege must leave one side open for escape (Maimonides, Laws of Kings 6:1–7). From the tree law they derived bal tashchit, the ban on needless destruction of anything useful (Shabbat 129a).
views.X: Christians have read these chapters in different ways: as history, as God's unique judgment in one time, or as allegory for spiritual warfare (Ephesians 6:12; Origen). Many today hold them alongside Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).

deep.title: Trees and people
deep.b: The question in 20:19 sets a limit on human destruction. Trees cannot run or fight; they are not the enemy. War is allowed against people who take up arms, but not against the land that will feed whoever lives there next. I read the verse as one of the Bible's earliest arguments from the nature of a thing to how it should be treated. This overlaps with the rabbinic principle of bal tashchit and with modern environmental readings of the verse.

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:1–6; Numbers 10:9; Joshua 6–11; Judges 7:3; 1 Samuel 15; 2 Kings 3:19, 25; 1 Maccabees 3:55–56; Matthew 5:44; Ephesians 6:10–17

settings.what: Rules for war
settings.to: Israel's army, its priest and its officials, when they go out to war in and beyond the land
settings.why: Before battle a priest tells the troops not to fear. Officials send home anyone with a new house, an unharvested vineyard or a new bride, and anyone afraid. Distant towns must first be offered peace. The towns of the land itself fall under the ban, so that their gods will not lead Israel astray. Even in a siege, fruit trees must be spared. The law limits war, puts it under God, and protects ordinary life.
views: Many scholars think these rules describe an ideal, perhaps from the 7th century BC, more than the actual practice of Israel's kings.

traditions.q: Moses gives Israel rules for war. May Christians fight in war?
views: Yes, but only in a just war: a defense against grave and lasting harm, as a last resort, with a real chance of success and without causing worse evils (Catechism 2309). These rules come from Augustine and Aquinas, and recent popes have grown more doubtful that modern wars can meet them.

War is sometimes necessary but never good. Basil the Great advised soldiers who had killed in war to stay away from communion for three years (Letter 188, canon 13), and the Orthodox have never adopted a full just war theory.
Christians may serve as soldiers and take part in just wars, because government is God's servant to restrain evil (Augsburg Confession, article 16; Romans 13:4).
Rulers may lawfully wage war on just and necessary occasions, and Christians may serve them (Westminster Confession 23.2).

The sword belongs to the world, outside the perfection of Christ, so Christians do not use it (Schleitheim Confession, article 6). Mennonites, Amish and Brethren refuse military service and read Israel's wars in light of Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).
Quakers declared to King Charles II in 1660 that they utterly deny all outward wars and fighting for any reason, because the Spirit of Christ never moves people to kill.

title: Blood, Captives and Sons
sum: When a body is found in the open country and no one knows the killer, the elders of the nearest town break a young cow's neck in a valley with a running stream, wash their hands over it, and declare, "Our hands did not shed this blood" (21:7). They pray for atonement, and the land is cleared.

The chapter then protects people with little power: a captive woman taken as a wife must be given a month to mourn and cannot be sold as a slave; the son of an unloved wife keeps the firstborn's double share. A stubborn and rebellious son may be brought by both parents to the elders. A criminal's body hung on a tree must be buried the same day, "for a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (21:23).
readings: Read as family law

Most of the chapter governs households: a captive wife, two wives, a rebellious son. Each law limits a husband's or father's power. Parents cannot punish a son themselves; they must go to the elders together.
Read as the land's purity
The chapter opens and closes with the land: innocent blood must be cleared from it, and a hanged body must not make it unclean. The land itself responds to how people live and die on it.

views.H: Moses gives laws for a settled society with towns, elders and family estates. The rite of the heifer teaches that a community bears some responsibility even for crimes it did not commit.
views.C: The heifer rite (21:1–9) seems very old, a magical removal of blood guilt that Deuteronomy reframes with priests and prayer. The rebellious-son law gives power to elders rather than fathers, a step toward public courts.
views.T: Hittite and Ugaritic texts make the town nearest a killing responsible to pay for it. Deuteronomy shares this idea of collective responsibility but turns it into a ritual of innocence and prayer.
views.J: The rabbis said that a rebellious son "never was and never will be" (Sanhedrin 71a), because the conditions they derived were nearly impossible to meet. The heifer rite ended when murderers multiplied (Mishnah Sotah 9:9).
views.X: Pilate's washing of his hands (Matthew 27:24) recalls the elders' rite. Paul quotes 21:23 to say "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13), and the Gospels note that Jesus' body was taken down before nightfall (John 19:31).

deep.b: The law speaks of a man already put to death and then hung on a tree for display, as Joshua did with the king of Ai (Joshua 8:29). By the time of the Dead Sea Scrolls the verse was applied to crucifixion, where the victim was hung alive. The Temple Scroll orders hanging for traitors (11QT 64:6–13). Paul's use of the verse for Jesus depends on that later meaning.

echoes: Genesis 4:10–11; Genesis 29:30–31; Numbers 35:33–34; Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:26–27; Proverbs 30:17; Matthew 27:24; Luke 15:11–32; John 19:31; Galatians 3:13

settings.what: An unsolved murder
settings.to: The elders and judges of the town nearest the body, and the Levite priests
settings.when: when a body is found in open country and no one knows the killer
settings.why: The elders break a young cow's neck in a valley with a running stream. They wash their hands over it and declare that they did not shed this blood. They pray for atonement. The problem the law answers is guilt that rests on the land when no one can be punished. It makes a town take responsibility for what happens near it.

settings.what: Family law: captive wives, the firstborn's share, a rebel son
settings.to: Israelite husbands and fathers, the women of their households, and the town elders at the gate
settings.why: Three laws limit a man's power in his household. A captive woman taken as a wife gets a month to mourn and cannot be sold as a slave. A father cannot give the firstborn's double share to the son of a wife he loves more. A rebellious son may be put to death only when both parents bring him to the elders. A teaching in the Talmud says that case never happened and never would, and that the law was given only to be studied. Rabbi Yonatan replied that he had seen one (Sanhedrin 71a).

settings.what: The body of a man who was hanged
settings.to: The community and its judges, after an execution
settings.why: The body must be buried the same day. One who is hanged is cursed by God, and the land must not be made unclean. Joshua keeps the rule (Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:27). Paul reads it of the cross (Galatians 3:13).

title: Your Brother's Ox, Your Neighbor's Wife
sum: A run of short laws covers daily life. Lost animals and goods must be returned: "do not hide yourself from them" (22:1). A fallen animal must be helped up. Men and women must not wear each other's clothing. A mother bird must be let go when her young are taken. A new house needs a railing on the roof. Seeds, plow animals and threads must not be mixed, and cloaks need tassels on four corners.

The second half concerns marriage and sexual crimes: a husband who falsely accuses his bride; adultery; a woman promised in marriage who lies with another man in town or is attacked in the country; and a man who seizes an unpromised virgin. The chapter ends with a ban on taking a father's wife.
readings: Read as neighborliness

The opening laws ask for small acts of care that cost time and effort: keeping a stray animal, lifting a fallen one, guarding a roof. They turn the command to love the neighbor into everyday practice.
Read with modern questions

The marriage laws raise hard questions about consent, virginity tests, and the value placed on women's sexuality. Readers differ on how far these laws protected women in their world and how far they reflect a culture that treated women as men's property.

views.H: Moses applies the covenant to the details of home and farm. The variety of the laws shows that no part of life is outside God's concern.
views.C: The chapter combines laws from different sources, some reworked from Exodus 23 and Leviticus 18–20. The marriage cases share a style with older Near Eastern law collections and may be among the oldest material in the code. Stephen Kaufman argued that the code follows the order of the Ten Commandments, with roughly 19:1–22:8 expanding "Do not murder" and 22:9–23:19 expanding "Do not commit adultery."
views.T: Treaty stipulations ranged from great loyalty to small duties of daily conduct. Read that way, care for a brother's lost ox and a safe roof are part of the covenant loyalty Israel owes its Lord, just as much as the ban on other gods.
views.J: The mother-bird law is called the "lightest" command, with the same reward as honoring parents, the "weightiest" (Yerushalmi Peah 1:1). The laws of mixtures became the tractate Kila'im, and the tassels the tsitsit still worn today.
views.X: Paul's "do not be unequally yoked" (2 Corinthians 6:14) may draw on 22:10. Jesus wore tassels (Matthew 9:20), and his teaching on adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28) deepens the law of 22:22.

deep.b: Verses 9–11 forbid sowing two kinds of seed in a vineyard, plowing with an ox and a donkey, and wearing wool and linen together. Leviticus 19:19 has similar rules. Readers have explained them as reflecting the order of creation "according to their kinds" (Genesis 1:11–25), as avoiding pagan practices, or as reserving mixtures for holy things, since the priests' garments mixed wool and linen.

echoes: Exodus 22:16–17; Exodus 23:4–5; Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 19:19; Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 15:37–41; Ruth 3:9; Matthew 9:20; John 8:3–11; 1 Corinthians 5:1; 2 Corinthians 6:14

settings.what: Neighbors, animals and keeping things apart
settings.to: Every Israelite, in daily life in the land
settings.why: A lost animal must be returned and a fallen one helped up: "do not hide yourself" (22:4). A mother bird must be let go. The householder who builds a new house must put a railing on the roof. Men and women must not wear each other's clothes. The farmer must not mix seeds or plow animals, and no one may weave mixed threads. The laws teach care for the neighbor and respect for the order God gave to creation.

settings.what: Marriage and sexual crimes
settings.to: Israelite men and women, their fathers, and the town elders who judge at the gate
settings.why: These laws cover a husband who falsely accuses his bride, and adultery. They cover a woman promised in marriage who is with another man in the town, or is attacked in the country. They cover a man who seizes an unpromised girl. They protect the family line and the household. In places they protect the woman too: the woman attacked in the open country is not punished. Modern readers find the father's role and the woman's lack of voice troubling.

title: Who May Enter
sum: The chapter opens with rules for "the assembly of the LORD": men who are castrated, those born of forbidden unions, and Ammonites and Moabites may not enter, but Edomites and Egyptians may after three generations. The army camp must be kept holy, with a place outside for relieving oneself, "For the LORD your God walks about in the middle of your camp" (23:14).

A runaway slave must not be handed back. No Israelite may become a shrine woman or shrine man, and earnings from prostitution may not pay a vow. Interest is forbidden between brothers. Vows must be kept. A passerby may eat from a neighbor's vineyard or field, but not carry anything away.
readings: Read as boundaries
The chapter sorts who belongs and how close they may come, from the assembly to the war camp. The lines are drawn by history (what Moab and Edom did) as well as by the body.
Read through later Scripture

Later books argue with these boundaries. Ruth the Moabite enters Israel and becomes David's ancestor. Isaiah promises eunuchs a name in God's house (Isaiah 56:3–5). Nehemiah enforces the Moabite law strictly (Nehemiah 13:1–3). The Bible holds this debate within itself.

views.H: Moses gives these rules from memory of the journey: Moab and Ammon refused bread and hired Balaam; Edom is Israel's brother; Egypt gave Israel a home before it enslaved them.
views.C: Many scholars see the assembly rules as reflecting the post-exilic debates of Ezra and Nehemiah over who belonged to Israel. Others think they are older laws about who could join the gathered tribes in war and worship.
views.T: "Never seek their peace or their good" (23:6) uses the vocabulary of treaty friendship. Israel must make no alliance with Ammon and Moab.
views.J: The rabbis limited the Moabite law to men, which allowed Ruth's marriage (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3). They debated what counts as a mamzer and worked to reduce such cases. The interest law shaped Jewish business ethics, with the heter iska partnership allowing investment without forbidden interest.
views.X: Philip baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch (Acts 8:26–39), and Paul says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). The disciples' picking grain on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1) relies on 23:25.

deep.b: Hammurabi's laws punished with death anyone who sheltered a runaway slave (Laws 15–16), and treaties required kings to return each other's fugitives. Deuteronomy 23:15–16 says the slave may live "in the place he chooses in one of your towns, wherever he likes. Do not mistreat him." Few ancient laws go so far.

deep.title: The assembly and the stranger
deep.b: The assembly rules in 23:1–8 and the welcome of the runaway slave in 23:15–16 sit in the same chapter. The first keeps some out; the second takes a runaway in without asking. I read the chapter as holding two concerns that never fully resolve: the purity of the community and its compassion. Later Scripture keeps negotiating between them. This overlaps with scholars who read Ruth and Isaiah 56 as answers to 23:1–8.

echoes: Genesis 19:30–38; Genesis 38:21; Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 15:16; Leviticus 25:35–37; Numbers 22–24; Ruth 1:16; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Isaiah 56:3–5; Matthew 12:1; Acts 8:26–39

settings.what: Who may enter the assembly of the LORD
settings.to: The assembly of Israel, and those outside it who seek to join
settings.why: Some men and some peoples may not enter the assembly. Ammonites and Moabites may never enter, for they would not help Israel in the wilderness and they hired Balaam. Edomites and Egyptians may enter after three generations. The law answers who belongs to Israel's worship. It stands behind Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13:1–3. The book of Ruth tells of a Moabite who became David's ancestor (Ruth 4:17).

settings.what: Keeping the war camp holy
settings.to: Israel's soldiers in the army camp
settings.when: when Israel goes out against its enemies
settings.why: The camp must be kept clean, with a place outside it to relieve oneself. The reason: "the LORD your God walks about in the middle of your camp" (23:14). Holiness reaches even the latrine, because God is present in the camp.

settings.what: Runaway slaves, vows, interest and a neighbor's field
settings.to: Every Israelite: slave owners, lenders, worshipers, and travelers
settings.why: A slave who escapes to Israel must not be handed back. No Israelite may be a shrine woman or shrine man. No interest may be charged to a fellow Israelite, though it may be charged to a foreigner (23:20). The ban binds Israelites in dealings with each other. Vows must be kept. A passerby may eat grain or grapes from a neighbor's field but not carry any away. The laws protect the weak and balance need with the rights of the owner.

title: Pledges, Wages and the Forgotten Sheaf
sum: The chapter opens with a case of divorce: a man who sends his wife away with a certificate may not remarry her after she has married another. A new husband is free from war for a year "to bring joy to the wife he has married" (24:5).

Most of the chapter protects the weak. Millstones may not be taken as a pledge. Kidnapping is a capital crime. A lender must not enter a borrower's house, and a poor man's coat must be returned by night. Day laborers, Israelite or foreign, are paid before sundown. Children are not put to death for their parents. Justice must not be bent for the foreigner or orphan, and a widow's garment may not be taken. Forgotten sheaves, olives and grapes belong to the poor. Twice the reason is given: "Remember that you were a slave" (24:18, 22).
readings: Read as dignity

Many of these laws protect self-respect as well as survival: the borrower brings out his own pledge; the worker is paid before night; the gleaner is given what was left on purpose. The poor are treated as neighbors, not projects.
Read as memory
The chapter's motive is history. Israel was once a slave, a foreigner and poor. That memory becomes law: what was done for Israel in Egypt must be done by Israel for others.

views.H: Moses gives Israel practical laws for a farming people, adding detail to the commands about pledges and wages given at Sinai (Exodus 22:26–27; Leviticus 19:13).
views.C: The chapter reworks laws from Exodus and Leviticus with Deuteronomy's characteristic motive clauses. The rule against punishing children (24:16) is quoted in 2 Kings 14:6, one of the few places where a law of Deuteronomy is cited by name in the history books.
views.T: Ancient Near Eastern kings boasted of protecting widows and orphans, as Hammurabi does in his epilogue. Deuteronomy gives that royal duty to every Israelite household.
views.J: The Mishnah's debate over divorce grounds (Mishnah Gittin 9:10) grows from 24:1. The forgotten sheaf (shikhechah) is treated in Mishnah Pe'ah 5–7, and the rabbis praised the man who rejoiced at forgetting one because it gave him a chance to keep a command.
views.X: Jesus' teaching on divorce answers a question rooted in this chapter (Matthew 19:3–9). James warns the rich that the wages they withheld "cry out" (James 5:4), and the parable of the vineyard workers pays wages at evening (Matthew 20:8).

deep.b: A pottery letter from Mesad Hashavyahu, near Yavneh-Yam on the coast, dated about 630 BC, records a harvester's complaint. He says his garment was taken although he had finished his work, and asks the official to return it. The letter shows ordinary people appealing to the kind of justice these laws describe.

echoes: Exodus 21:16; Exodus 22:21–27; Leviticus 19:9–10, 13; Numbers 12:10–15; Ruth 2; 2 Kings 14:6; Jeremiah 3:1; Ezekiel 18:20; Matthew 19:3–9; James 5:4

settings.what: No remarriage after a second marriage
settings.to: Israelite husbands and wives, in cases of divorce
settings.why: A man who divorces his wife with a certificate may not take her back after she has married another. The law assumes divorce and limits it. Jesus and the rabbis argued about the grounds it names (Matthew 19:3–9), and the Mishnah's tractate Gittin records the rabbis' debate.

settings.what: Protecting the newly married, the borrower, the worker and the poor
settings.to: Israelite employers, lenders, landowners and judges, in the land
settings.why: A new husband is free from war for a year. A millstone may not be taken as a pledge. A lender may not enter a borrower's house, and a poor man's coat must be returned by night. Workers, Israelite or foreign, are paid before sundown. Children are not put to death for their parents' crimes. Forgotten sheaves, olives and grapes are left for the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. Twice the reason is given: remember that you were a slave in Egypt (24:18, 22). The book of Ruth shows the gleaning law at work.

traditions.q: Moses allowed divorce (24:1–4). May divorced Christians marry again?
views: A valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by anyone but death, so a divorced Catholic who remarries without an annulment may not receive communion (Catechism 1650). An annulment declares that a true marriage never existed. Pope Francis's Amoris Laetitia (2016) opened a path of case-by-case discernment, which Catholics still debate.
Marriage is meant to be one and lifelong, but the church, by mercy ("economy"), may allow a second and even a third marriage after divorce, with a service of a more penitent tone.
Luther allowed divorce and remarriage for adultery and for desertion, and also urged reconciliation where possible (The Estate of Marriage, 1522).
Adultery (Matthew 19:9) and willful desertion that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15) are the only grounds for divorce, and the innocent party may remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6).

Many Mennonite, Amish and other Anabaptist groups have taught that a divorced person may not remarry while the former spouse is alive, reading Jesus' words in Mark 10:11–12 strictly. More progressive Mennonite churches now allow it.

title: Honest Weights and a Brother's Name
sum: A guilty man may be beaten, but no more than forty blows, so that "your brother will be shamed" no more (25:3). An ox must not be muzzled while threshing. When a man dies without a son, his brother should marry the widow so that the dead man's name lives on; a brother who refuses is shamed at the gate by the widow, who pulls off his sandal.

A woman who seizes a man's private parts in a fight is punished by losing her hand. Merchants must not keep "two kinds of weights" (25:13). The chapter ends with Amalek, who attacked the weary stragglers in the desert: "wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky. Do not forget!" (25:19).
readings: Read as fairness

Most of the laws here limit power: the judge who might beat too hard, the farmer who would starve his ox, the brother who keeps his dead brother's land, the merchant with false weights. Each is held to a measure.
Read as remembering
The chapter ends with memory of a cruel enemy and a command not to forget. The laws before it guard the weak in Israel; Amalek is remembered as the one who preyed on the weak.

views.H: Moses gives laws for justice in court and market, and closes the code's ethical section by recalling an event from the wilderness that Israel witnessed (Exodus 17).
views.C: The levirate law and the hand law look old and have close parallels in Middle Assyrian and Hittite laws. The Amalek passage may have been added to connect the law code to the stories of Saul (1 Samuel 15).
views.T: Honest weights and measures were the business of kings in the ancient world, and Mesopotamian law collections often speak of them. Here the LORD himself is the guardian of fair trade.
views.J: The Mishnah set lashes at thirty-nine (Mishnah Makkot 3:10). The Sifre turned the hand penalty into a payment for shame. The Amalek verses are read on Shabbat Zakhor, and the sandal ceremony, chalitsah, is still practiced.
views.X: Paul applies 25:4 to paying ministers (1 Corinthians 9:9; 1 Timothy 5:18), and the Sadducees question Jesus with the levirate law (Matthew 22:23–33). Paul received "forty lashes less one" five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

deep.b: Archaeologists have found hundreds of small stone weights from Judah, many marked with a sign for the shekel and numbers for 2, 4 or 8 shekels. They vary from the standard by several percent, which shows how easy it was for a dishonest trader to keep a heavy weight for buying and a light one for selling.

echoes: Genesis 38; Exodus 17:8–16; Leviticus 19:35–36; Ruth 4:1–12; 1 Samuel 15; Proverbs 11:1; Amos 8:5; Matthew 22:23–33; 1 Corinthians 9:9; 2 Corinthians 11:24; 1 Timothy 5:18

settings.what: Limits on punishment; the threshing ox
settings.to: Judges, and every Israelite farmer
settings.why: A guilty man may be beaten no more than forty blows, so that he is not degraded. An ox must not be muzzled while it threshes. Both laws keep dignity in place even for the guilty and the beast. Paul applies the ox law to those who work for the church (1 Corinthians 9:9).

settings.what: Brother-in-law marriage
settings.to: Brothers who live together, a widow with no son, and the town elders at the gate
settings.why: When a man dies without a son, his brother should marry the widow so that the dead man's name lives on (25:6). A brother who refuses is shamed at the gate by the widow, who pulls off his sandal. The law protects the widow and the dead man's name, and with it, many think, the family's land. Ruth 4 and Genesis 38 show related customs.

settings.what: A shameful act in a fight; honest weights
settings.to: Israelites in daily life, and merchants in the market
settings.why: A woman who seizes a man's private parts in a fight is punished. Merchants must not keep two kinds of weights or measures, one for buying and one for selling. Honest trade, like honest courts, is a condition for long life in the land.
views: Walsh argues that the punishment in 25:12 may mean shaving or shaming, not cutting off a hand; most translations keep the hand.

settings.what: Remember Amalek
settings.to: All Israel, once the LORD has given it rest in the land
settings.why: Amalek attacked the weak and weary stragglers at the rear on the road from Egypt. When Israel has rest, it must wipe out Amalek's memory. The law closes the code with a memory of those who preyed on the weak. Jews read it on the Sabbath before Purim, because Haman is called an Agagite (Esther 3:1).

title: A Basket of First Fruits
sum: When Israel is settled in the land, each farmer is to bring the first of his harvest in a basket to the chosen place and recite a short history before the LORD: "My father was a wandering Aramean" (26:5). Jacob's family went down to Egypt, became a nation, was oppressed, cried out, and was brought out "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" into "a land flowing with milk and honey" (26:8–9). Then he sets the basket down, bows, and rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner.

In the third year, after giving the tithe to the poor, the farmer declares that he has done so and asks God to "Look down from your holy dwelling, from the heavens, and bless your people Israel" (26:15). The law code closes with a covenant declaration: Israel affirms the LORD as its God, and the LORD affirms Israel as his "own private treasure" (26:18).
readings: Read as liturgy
These are two of the few set prayers in the Torah. A farmer, not a priest, speaks. He tells the story as his own, "us" and "we," and turns a harvest gift into a confession of faith.
Read as covenant
The final verses (26:16–19) are a formal agreement, with each side declaring its part. The law code ends where Sinai began: a holy people, treasured by God.

views.H: Moses gives Israel words to speak in the land they have not yet entered. The first-fruits prayer looks back to the patriarchs and forward to the settlement, joining every generation to the exodus.
views.C: Gerhard von Rad thought 26:5–9 was an ancient creed at the root of the Pentateuch. Most scholars now read it as Deuteronomy's own summary of the story, though built on older traditions.
views.T: Covenant ceremonies ended with mutual declarations. 26:16–19 reads like such a ratification, leading into the blessings and curses of chapters 27–28, the expected next section of a treaty.
views.J: The Passover Haggadah builds its telling of the exodus on 26:5–8, reading "an Aramean tried to destroy my father" of Laban. The Mishnah tractate Bikkurim describes the joyful procession of baskets to Jerusalem.
views.X: Paul calls the risen Christ "the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Peter applies the treasured-people language to the church (1 Peter 2:9), and James calls believers "a kind of first fruits" of God's creatures (James 1:18).

deep.b: The opening words, arammi oved avi, have been read in at least three ways: "my father was a wandering (or perishing) Aramean," usually of Jacob; "my father left Aram," in the Greek; and "an Aramean tried to destroy my father," in the Targum, the Vulgate and the Haggadah. See the variant on 26:5. All three readings agree that Israel's story begins with a small, threatened family far from home.

echoes: Genesis 28:5; Genesis 31; Genesis 46:3; Exodus 1:8–14; Exodus 6:6–7; Exodus 19:5–6; Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 26:12; Joshua 24:2–13; 1 Corinthians 15:20; 1 Peter 2:9

settings.what: First fruits and the farmer's creed
settings.to: Every Israelite farmer, once he has land and his first harvest, at the chosen place
settings.when: at the first harvest in the land
settings.why: The farmer brings a basket of first fruits to the priest and recites a short history. It begins, "My father was a wandering Aramean" (26:5). It goes down to Egypt, out by the LORD's strong hand, and into a land flowing with milk and honey. Then he rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner. The prayer makes each farmer say that his land is a gift. Jews retell this passage at the Passover meal.
views: Von Rad called 26:5–9 a short historical creed, among the oldest parts of the Torah.
An Aramean tried to destroy my father
The Targum Onkelos and the Passover Haggadah read the opening words as "Laban the Aramean sought to destroy my father," so the creed begins with Jacob rescued from Laban.
Many scholars now think it is a Deuteronomic summary of the story, written for this ceremony.

settings.what: The third-year tithe declaration
settings.by: Moses (giving the words the farmer is to say)
settings.to: Every Israelite farmer, before the LORD, after the tithe of the third year
settings.when: in the third year, the year of the tithe for the poor
settings.why: First the farmer gives the tithe to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Then he declares that he has done so and kept it pure. He asks God to look down from heaven and bless his people and the land. Care for the poor becomes a prayer said aloud before God.

settings.what: The covenant declared today
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: at the close of the law code
settings.why: Today Israel has affirmed that the LORD is its God, and today the LORD has affirmed that Israel is his own private treasure. The two statements seal the code as a covenant. The word "today" puts each later hearer in the moment of choosing.
